summary: This informational RFC analyzes whether Loop-Free Alternates, a method of IP fast reroute, work in service provider core and access networks. It covers link and node failures and gives guidance for topologies, especially the access network.

eli5.summary: If a road closes, routers want an instant backup route that does not loop. This looks at when that works well.

questions: lfa in service provider access networks
what is a loop free alternate
does lfa work in access networks
subtitle: Where pre-computed backup next hops (Loop-Free Alternates) work well in service provider access and core networks, and where they do not.

tldr.problem: Service providers want traffic to be repaired quickly when a link or node fails, but need to know whether the simple Loop-Free Alternate (LFA) method of IP fast reroute actually gives enough protection in their topologies.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyzes four common access topologies (triangle, full mesh, square and extended U) link by link, runs a simulation on 11 real core topologies, and discusses design rules, simplicity benefits and capacity-planning tool support.
tldr.outcome: Access and aggregation topologies get excellent link and node LFA coverage, while core coverage varies widely from topology to topology and must be assessed case by case.

today: RFC 6571 is Informational and the metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It is an applicability analysis of the LFA method defined in RFC 5286, not a protocol specification.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
This document analyzes the applicability of the Loop-Free Alternate (LFA) method of providing IP fast reroute (IPFRR), defined in RFC 5286 and the framework in RFC 5714, in the core and access parts of Service Provider networks. It considers both link and node failures and gives guidance on which network topologies suit LFAs, with special emphasis on the access part of the network.

It uses IS-IS as the reference, and says the analysis applies equally to OSPF. It assumes all protected links are point-to-point and that normal routing follows the shortest path.
sections.eli5: Routers can pre-pick a backup road in case their main road breaks. This document asks how often that trick works for big internet providers.

sections.title: LFA Definitions
sections.content:
A per-prefix LFA for a destination D at a node S is a pre-computed backup IGP next hop for that destination. A neighbor N is a link-protecting LFA if ND < NS + SD, where XY is the IGP distance from X to Y. It is node-protecting for a route with initial next hop F if it is link-protecting and also satisfies ND < NF + FD.

A de facto node-protecting LFA is a link-protecting one that turns out to protect against node failure anyway, for example when several LFAs activated by neighbors of the failed node together send traffic on to a safe neighbor. A per-link LFA is a single backup next hop for all destinations reached through a link. Finally, a micro-loop (uLoop) is a transient forwarding loop during a routing transition, as defined in RFC 5715.

The RFC illustrates all of this with an example topology and shows that a per-link LFA can fail to give de facto node protection: in its example, after node C fails, the chosen backup E activates its own backup, which points back to S, and traffic loops.
sections.eli5: A backup road is only safe if it does not lead straight back through the broken spot. A router checks this with a simple distance rule before it picks the backup.

sections.title: Access Network Topologies
sections.content:
The access part of the network is often the majority of nodes and links. It is organized in several tens or more of regions joined by the core, and each region is typically built from a common template. The analysis takes one access region with two routers C1 and C2 linking it to the core, aggregation routers A1 and A2, and edge routers E1 and E2. It assumes the design rules c < d + u and a < d + u, and c < a for the square.

It then examines four topologies, failing each link and node in turn: triangle (edges dual-homed to C1 and C2), full mesh, square and extended U (the last three with edges attached to A1 and A2). Per-prefix and per-link LFAs are both evaluated.

The results: intra-area link protection is full in every topology, except that in the square C1 has no LFA for destination A1. Node protection is available for intra-area destinations in all four. For inter-area destinations, link protection is full everywhere, and node protection depends on the metric difference e between the two core routers' paths to the destination, for example needing e < c in the triangle.
sections.eli5: Provider networks are built from copies of a few small map shapes. The authors check each shape one broken road at a time and find that nearly every break has a safe backup.

sections.title: Design Rules That Improve Coverage
sections.content:
Two design choices improve node protection for destinations outside the region. In a dual-plane core, each access region connects to plane 1 and plane 2 through its two C routers, and e = 0, which improves LFA node-protection coverage in all analyzed topologies. In a two-tiered IGP metric allocation, all L2 metrics fall in a range R1 and all L1 metrics in a range R2, with R1 much smaller than R2. This guarantees c < a, e < c and e < a.

On micro-loops, the RFC finds that in the square design a transient loop can occur for traffic to A1 when link C1A1 fails, because C1 reroutes to C2, which initially reaches A1 through C1 as c < a. In the other analyzed transitions, rerouting nodes deviate traffic to adjacent nodes whose paths do not change, so no micro-loop can form.
sections.eli5: If the planners choose the road lengths with care, backups work almost everywhere and the detours do not accidentally send cars in circles.

sections.title: Core Network Results
sections.content:
Core networks are harder. Their design is driven by cost, latency and bandwidth, constrained by fiber availability, and optimizing for local IP restoration is likely a non-primary goal. The RFC describes three profiles. If resilience is planned on IGP convergence, LFA is a free bonus: where an LFA exists the loss of connectivity is likely reduced by a factor of 10 (50 msec versus 500 msec). If the designer wants very high, deterministic coverage but cannot engineer the topology, LFA should not be considered and MPLS TE FRR would perform much better. If the designer wants deterministic coverage and does engineer the topology, LFA is appealing.

The simulation uses the link-state database from a core router on 11 real SP core topologies with from 16 to 600 nodes. Per-prefix LFA coverage ranges from 67% to 99% (average 89%, median 94%), and per-link coverage from 16% to 98% (average 67%, median 68%). Unlike in the access topologies, per-prefix LFA outperforms per-link LFA in the backbone. The RFC concludes that core applicability needs a case-by-case analysis.
sections.eli5: On the big highways between cities, the map is messier. Sometimes a backup road exists nearly everywhere, and sometimes it hardly ever does, so each provider has to check its own map.

sections.title: Simplicity and Capacity Planning
sections.content:
The RFC argues that LFA benefits stem from simplicity. It is automatic and part of the IGP with no extra configuration, needs no protocol change so it can be deployed router by router, pre-computes backup paths into the data plane, and gives link and node protection together. Compared with MPLS TE FRR it adds no virtual layer of tunnels to manage, and the per-prefix mode can spread fast-rerouted load over several repair paths. A repair time under 50 msec is achievable with a fast enough FIB update, and with a prefix-independent implementation repair time does not scale with the number of destinations.

It also describes what an LFA-aware capacity-planning tool should offer: coverage estimation per link and per prefix, coverage weighted by traffic, verification for a given set of demands, and what-if scenarios for failures such as a single SRLG failure, covering both LFA coverage and link load. The RFC stresses that LFAs are not meant to replace MPLS TE FRR, and the two schemes in the core and access are independent, so a design might use LFA in the access and MPLS TE FRR in the core.

On security, the RFC points to RFC 5286 and says this document introduces no new security considerations.
sections.eli5: The best thing about the backup-road trick is that it is easy: routers work it out on their own, and one router at a time can start using it. Planning tools can then warn about places where no backup exists.
